ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: All procedures were approved by the IRB at anonymized for review.
This research received approval from the Institutional Review Board at (anonymized for review).
Experiment 1 Method Participants Participants were 54 undergraduate students from anonymized for review ages 18-22 (16 Men, 38 Women) who participated for partial course credit.

Participants were randomly assigned to one of two conditions that varied in how multisensory category information was presented during training (Simultaneous [10 Men, 17 Women], Separate [6 Men, 21 Women]).
All participants completed an identical generalization test after training.
Participants completed the study in person using the Gorilla Experiment Builder (Anwyl-Irvine et al., 2020).
After stimulus presentation, participants were prompted to respond which category the audiovisual stimuli belonged to by pressing the 1 or 2 keys on the keyboard.
Participants had an unlimited amount of time to respond.
Finally, we added attention checks throughout training to ensure that participants were attending to both modalities throughout the task.
Participants were 132 undergraduate students from anonymized for review ages 18-26 ( 20Men, 112 Women) who completed the study in person for partial course credit.

table.text: Participants were randomly assigned to one of four conditions varying in presentation format (Simultaneous, Separate) and total stimulus duration (Short [1 sec], Long [2 sec]): Simultaneous-Long (N = 34; 7 Men, 27 Women), Simultaneous-Short (N = 31; 5 Men, 26 Women), Separate-Long (N = 33; 5 Men, 28 Women), Separate-Short (N = 34; 3 Men, 31 Women).

The test procedure was similar to Experiment 1 except that participants completed more trials overall (auditory-only: N = 32, visual-only; N = 32, audiovisual congruent: N = 32, audiovisual incongruent: N = 32), only near transfer stimuli were used, and presentation and duration were counterbalanced across trials.

At the end of the experiment, as exploratory measures, participants were asked how they used modality information to make decisions during learning and whether they thought the modalities were related to each other (see Supplemental Materials).
Participants were 180 adults recruited online from Prolific ages 18-64 (95 Men, 85 Women) who completed the study online for a small payment ($10).
Participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions varying in presentation format (Simultaneous, Separate, Unisensory).
All participants completed the same test procedure as Experiment 2 with auditory-only, visual-only, audiovisualseparate, and audiovisual-simultaneous trial types.
Participants completed the same exploratory questionnaire measures as Experiment 2 (see Supplementary Materials).

When participants were trained on the visual modality, responses were aligned more with the visual than auditory modality (M = 0.28, t(36) = -8.02, p < .0001, d = -1.32) which was significantly different from all other conditions (ps < .0001).

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: To account for possible alternative explanations for the results in Experiment 1, we made several changes to Experiment 2. First, while stimuli in the two conditions were identical, conditions differed in both how stimuli were presented and the total stimulus duration such that differences could be due to the relatively short time Simultaneous learners had to process the stimuli (1 sec) compared to Separate learners (1 sec + 1 sec = 2 sec). In Experiment 2, we disentangle these explanations by separately manipulating presentation format and stimulus duration. Second, all audiovisual test stimuli were presented simultaneously, potentially introducing an unintended familiarity benefit in the Simultaneous condition. In Experiment 2, we counterbalance the presentation and duration of test trials to not unfairly advantage any condition. Third, while the pattern of responses for incongruent stimuli was qualitatively different in the two conditions (d = 0.35), the overall effect was not significant. Given the observed effect size, we were underpowered to observe a difference (sensitivity analysis indicated that our sample size could detect an effect of d = 0.78 or larger with 80% power). In Experiment 2, we collect a higher-powered sample given the effect sizes observed in Experiment 1. Finally, we added attention checks throughout training to ensure that participants were attending to both modalities throughout the task. Experiment 2 was pre-registered and we report all planned confirmatory analyses (https://osf.io/meuyh/overview?view_only=a029de89132248439c6c35b4968a0bed).

table.title: How Presentation Shapes Multisensory Category Learning
table.research_questions:
1. If the results of our previous study replicate and presentation format does not impact multisensory category learning, there will be no differences in training accuracy when auditory and visual category information is presented simultaneously or separately. 

2. If the results of our previous study replicate and presentation format affects multisensory category generalization, generalization test accuracy will be higher overall when information was presented simultaneously during training compared to separately.  

3. If the results of our previous study replicate and different presentation formats encourage different kinds of attention to stimulus information, there will be a significant interaction between training presentation (simultaneous, separate) and generalization test trial type (audiovisual, auditory-only, visual-only). When information was presented simultaneously during training, participants will perform better in the test when auditory information is present (audiovisual, auditory-only) than when only visual information is present. In contrast, when information was presented separately during training, participants will not perform differently across test trial types. 

4. If the results of our previous study replicate and different presentation formats encourage different kinds of attention to stimulus information, participants trained with information presented simultaneously during training will have responses to incongruent audiovisual stimuli that are more aligned with the auditory stimulus category than the visual stimulus category, while those trained with information presented separately will have responses to incongruent audiovisual stimuli aligned with neither auditory nor visual. We hypothesize that in this higher-powered sample, this difference will be significant indicating an attentional bias in the simultaneous training condition. 

Critically, this new experiment will enable testing different competing hypotheses about the source of this attentional bias: 

A. If multisensory presentation of the information drives the attentional bias, then simultaneous presentation will produce a stronger auditory bias than separate presentation, regardless of whether information was presented at relatively short or long stimulus durations. 

B. If attentional demand due to relatively short stimulus presentation times drives the attentional bias in the simultaneous training condition, then short total stimulus duration (1000 ms) will produce stronger auditory bias than long duration (2000 ms), regardless of whether information was presented simultaneously or separately during training.

C. If multisensory presentation and attentional demand due to relatively short stimulus presentations both impact attentional biases, we may expect:
C1. Significant independent effects of presentation type during training (simultaneous, separate) and presentation duration (short, long). 
C2. Significant interaction between these factors. While there are many possible patterns of interactions, we pose that a likely pattern we would find is that any type of training that presents information separately across modalities will not result in an attention bias (regardless of short or long stimulus presentation) but that training that presents information simultaneously will result in a stronger attention bias when information is presented for a relatively short duration compared to a long duration. 

D. If neither presentation type nor stimulus duration impact attentional biases, we expect to see no differences in accuracy across test trial types and responses that are not aligned with either the auditory or visual modality for incongruent stimuli, with no differences across conditions.
table.study_type: Experiment - A researcher randomly assigns treatments to study subjects, this includes field or lab experiments. This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials.
table.blinding: For studies that involve human subjects, they will not know the treatment group to which they have been assigned. Personnel who interact directly with the study subjects (either human or non-human subjects) will not be aware of the assigned treatments. (Commonly known as “double blind”)
table.study_design_overview: Mixed design varying presentation timing (simultaneous vs. separate, between-subjects) and total duration of stimulus presentation (short vs, long, between-subjects). In training, training block (1-8, within-subjects). In test, stimulus type (auditory, visual, audiovisual, within-subjects) + incongruent audiovisual. We will counterbalance the order of presentation of modalities for separate trials (auditory-visual or visual-auditory), assignment of category to response key mapping (category A = 1 and B = 2 or category A = 2 and B = 1), whether audiovisual test stimuli are presented separately or simultaneously, and the duration (short/long) of the test stimuli.
table.randomization: Participants will be randomly assigned to one of four conditions that vary in presentation timing (Simultaneous, Separate) and total stimulus duration (1000 ms [short], 2000 ms [long]) using a randomization node in Gorilla Experiment Builder (Anwyl-Irvine et al., 2020). Within each participant, trial order in both training and test will be randomized using rowwise randomization in the spreadsheet in Gorilla's Task Builder.
table.existing_data: Registration prior to creation of data
table.data_collection_procedures: Participants will be undergraduate students from the University of New Hampshire, between the ages of 18 to 65, who will participate for partial course credit using the SONA Psychology Subject Pool. Participants will be required to self-report normal or corrected-to-normal hearing and vision.
table.sample_size_rationale: The target number of participants was determined via a series of power analyses using WebPower (Zhang & Yuan, 2018) based on the results of an initial Experiment 1 (which was not pre-registered). We wanted to be sure we can detect the size of effect in the analysis of attention bias across conditions from the audiovisual-incongruent stimuli (d = 0.35) that was not statistically significant in Experiment 1. To detect an effect size of d = 0.35 for an independent samples t-test, with an alpha of .05 and power of 80%, 65 participants would be needed in each condition (Separate and Simultaneous). Next, we wanted to be sure we can detect the most complex interaction in our planned analyses of presentation timing (2, between-subjects), total duration (2, between-subjects), and stimulus type (3, within-subjects). Using the sample size determined from the first power analysis (and rounding to have equal numbers in the groups), with 33 participants per individual condition with alpha of .05, power of 80%, the smallest possible observable interaction effect size we would be able to observe is relatively small (f = 0.16). Therefore, we are confident that this sample size would be able to detect possible a three-way interaction and so we plan to recruit 33 participants per condition for a total of 132 participants.
table.manipulated_variables:
- presentation timing during training (2, between-subjects) - Simultaneous (presenting at the same time) or Separate (separately with modality order counterbalanced across trials) presentation of audiovisual category stimuli
- total stimulus duration during training (2, between-subjects) -  short duration trials (1000ms) or long duration trials (2000ms) for all audiovisual stimuli during training. Note this is total duration: Separate short (500 + 500), Simultaneous short (1000), Separate long (1000 + 1000), Simultaneous long (2000). 
- training block (1-8, within-subjects) - 25 trials per block
- stimulus type in test (3, within-subjects) -- auditory-only, visual-only, audiovisual. 
- incongruent audiovisual stimulus type in test
table.measured_variables:
Accuracy and reaction time on each trial. For incongruent stimuli, whether their response aligned with the category identity of the auditory stimulus or visual stimulus. Participants will answer the following questions in a post-experiment questionnaire: 

1. Which of the following best describes how you approached the learning part of the task (where you received feedback about your responses)?
- I primarily used the auditory information to make my decision.
- I primarily used the visual information to make my decision.
- I used both auditory and visual information to make my decision.
- Other - please specify:

2. Which of the following do you think is true?
- The auditory and visual information are related to each other.
- The auditory and visual information are NOT related to each other.
- I am not sure whether the auditory and visual information were related or not.
table.indices:
Mean accuracy and reaction time across each block of 25 trials will be calculated for training. 

Mean accuracy and reaction times for each trial type (auditory only, visual only, audiovisual) will be calculated for the generalization test. We will collapse all trials of these stimulus types (regardless of presentation type or duration) in the main analyses. 

Mean proportion of responses aligned with auditory modality category identity will be calculated for audiovisual incongruent stimuli in the generalization test.
table.statistical_tests:
Training phase. Mixed-model ANOVAs will be conducted to examine the effects of presentation timing (Separate vs. Simultaneous; between-subjects), total duration of stimulus presentation (1000 ms [short] vs. 2000 ms [long]; between-subjects), and block (1-8; within-subjects) on accuracy. Any significant main effects or interactions from the ANOVAs will be explored further with Bonferroni-corrected post-hoc tests.

Test phase. We will examine generalization accuracy using a mixed-model ANOVA with effects of presentation timing (Separate vs. Simultaneous; between-subjects), total duration of stimulus presentation (1000 ms [short] vs. 2000 ms [long]; between-subjects), and trial type (auditory-only, visual-only, audiovisual-congruent; within-subjects). If there are any significant interactions or a main effect of trial type, we will focus our interpretations on comparisons of single modality (auditory-only, visual-only) vs. audiovisual (as evidence of potential multisensory categorization benefits) and auditory-only vs. visual-only (as evidence of attentional bias). 

We will compute the second measure of attentional bias from audiovisual-incongruent trials by using the proportion of responses aligned with the auditory modality minus the proportion of responses aligned with the visual modality. Attentional bias will be assessed within each group separately using one-sample t-tests against chance level (0.50). We will also compare attentional biases across groups using a 2x2 between-subjects ANOVA to examine the effects of presentation timing (Separate vs. Simultaneous) and total duration stimulus presentation (1000 ms [short] vs. 2000 ms [long]).
table.inference_criteria: We will use the standard p < .05 criteria for determining if the ANOVA, t-tests, and the post hoc tests suggest that the results are significantly different from those expected if the null hypothesis were correct. The post-hoc Bonferroni test adjusts for multiple comparisons.
table.data_exclusion_criteria:
We will include attention checks in both auditory and visual modalities where participants will need to rapidly (<2 seconds) press the spacebar when hearing a brief pure tone or seeing a "Press the spacebar" prompt on the screen. We will only include participants who perform above 85% on these attention checks in both modalities.  

Outliers will be included in the analyses.
table.missing_data_handling: If a participant does not complete all category learning and generalization test trials, they will not be included in the analyses.
table.exploratory_analyses: We will analyze whether there were differences based on the counterbalancing of trial types in the test by varying the presentation type (simultaneous, separate) of audiovisual trials (both congruent or incongruent) or the total presentation duration (short/long) of auditory-only, visual-only, or audiovisual trials (both congruent or incongruent). We counterbalanced these variables to ensure that no specific conditions were favored by having test trials that matched the presentation type experienced during training. We have a weak hypothesis that participants may perform better when the stimulus types match what they experienced during training, but will analyze this as an exploratory analysis due to the small number of trials of each type and the likely lack of power to see many-factor interactions beyond those targeted in our main theoretically-driven analyses. We will also examine answers to the post-test questionnaire and how they may relate to the modality bias or learning outcomes as exploratory analyses.

table.title: Multisensory compared to unisensory category learning
table.research_questions: We seek to replicate a previous experiment in an online sample comparing multisensory (audiovisual) category learning when the same stimulus information is presented simultaneously or separately within the same trial. Further, we compare multisensory learning with purely unisensory learning to understand potential benefits of multisensory training on generalization to novel unisensory or multisensory exemplars.
table.study_type: Randomized Experiment: Must include random assignment of subjects to treatments or conditions. This usually includes lab experiments, field experiments, intervention experiments, randomized controlled trials, and A/B testing.
table.blinding: Subjects will not be aware of the assigned treatment during data collection (either because the subjects are not human participants or because of blinding procedures).
table.study_design_overview: Participants will complete a headphone check. Participants will be randomly assigned to one of three presentation conditions (Multisensory-Separate, Multisensory-Simultaneous, Unisensory). Participants will then learn rule-based categories defined by auditory and/or visual information with corrective feedback presented on each trial. Multisensory categories are redundant across modalities. After training, participants will complete the same generalization test regardless of their training condition. The generalization test will present stimuli in all possible formats (audiovisual-separate, audiovisual-simultaneous, auditory only, visual only) with novel stimuli and participants will not receive feedback. We will counterbalance order of presentation of modalities for separate trials during both training and test and assignment of category to response key mapping (category A = 1 and B = 2 or category A = 2 and B = 1). We will also present audiovisual trials in the test that contain incongruent auditory and visual information to understand how learners attend to modality information to make categorization decisions. Finally, participants will be asked how they made category decisions (auditory only, visual only, both auditory and visual) and whether they thought the auditory and visual information were related to one another and, if so, how.
table.randomization: Assignment to condition will be randomized using the counterbalance node in Gorilla Experiment Builder (Anwyl-Irvine et al., 2020) with ratios to get approximately equal numbers of participants in the Simultaneous, Separate, and Unisensory conditions. For Unisensory conditions, participants will be randomly assigned to learn visual or auditory categories. Trials will be presented in a random order within training and within test using the randomize trials option in the spreadsheets in Gorilla.
table.data_collection_procedures: Data will be collected on Prolific using the following inclusion/eligibility criteria: 18-65 years old, normal hearing, normal or corrected-to-normal vision. Data is anticipated to be collected in June 2026 and take approximately 1 week.
table.sample_size: We will collect data until we have obtained complete data from 180 participants who pass all attention checks > 85%, with 60 participants per between-subjects condition.
table.sample_size_rationale: The sample size was chosen based on the prior experiment that we are replicating/extending. Specifically, to observe an effect size of f = 0.16 of the most complex expected interaction in our planned analyses of presentation condition (3, between-subjects) and test stimulus type (4, within-subjects), a power analysis conducted in WebPower in R (Zhang & Yuan, 2018) indicated that we would need a sample size of 179 to observe this effect size with alpha of .05 and power of 80%. We rounded to 180 to reach equal number of participants across presentation type conditions (n = 60).

Training block (within subjects)

Generalization test trial types (within subjects)
-	Audiovisual-separate (congruent)
-	Audiovisual-simultaneous (congruent)
-	Audiovisual-separate (incongruent)
-	Audiovisual-simultaneous (incongruent)
-	Auditory only
-	Visual only
table.measured_variables:
Accuracy will be assessed on each trial and then averaged across blocks (training) or trial type (test) for analyses. 

For audiovisual-incongruent test trials, proportion of responses aligned with trained modality will be assessed for Unisensory conditions (to account for counterbalancing across modalities) and proportion of responses aligned with auditory modality will be assessed for the Multisensory conditions. 


1. Which of the following best describes how you approached the learning part of the task (where you received feedback about your responses)? - I primarily used the auditory information to make my decision. - I primarily used the visual information to make my decision. - I used both auditory and visual information to make my decision. - Other - please specify: 2. Which of the following do you think is true? - The auditory and visual information are related to each other. - The auditory and visual information are NOT related to each other. - I am not sure whether the auditory and visual information were related or not.
table.indices: Mean accuracy and reaction time across each block of 25 trials will be calculated for training. Mean accuracy for each trial type (auditory only, visual only, audiovisual-separate, audiovisual-simultaneous) will be calculated for the generalization test. Mean proportion of responses aligned with auditory modality (Multisensory conditions) and trained modality (Unisensory conditions) category identity will be calculated for audiovisual incongruent stimuli in the generalization test.
table.statistical_tests:
Training phase. Mixed-model ANOVAs will be conducted to examine the effects of presentation format (Multisensory-Separate, Multisensory-Simultaneous, Unisensory; between-subjects) and block (1-8; within-subjects) on accuracy. Any significant main effects or interactions from the ANOVAs will be explored further with Bonferroni-corrected post-hoc tests. 

Test phase. We will examine generalization accuracy using a mixed-model ANOVA with effects of presentation format (Separate, Simultaneous, Unisensory; between-subjects) and trial type (auditory-only, visual-only, audiovisual-congruent-separate, audiovisual-congruent-simultaneous; within-subjects). For Unisensory conditions, only the trained modality will be included in the analyses (auditory-only or visual-only). If there are any significant interactions or a main effect of trial type, we will focus our interpretations on comparisons of single modality (auditory-only, visual-only) vs. audiovisual (as evidence of potential multisensory categorization benefits) and auditory-only vs. visual-only (as evidence of attentional bias). We will also test whether accuracy for the untrained modality in the Unisensory conditions is different from chance (50%) using one-sample t-tests. 

We will compute the second measure of attentional bias from audiovisual-incongruent trials by using the proportion of responses aligned with the auditory modality for multisensory conditions. For Unisensory conditions, we will compute the proportion of responses aligned with the trained modality. Attentional bias will be assessed within each group separately using one-sample t-tests against chance level (0.50). We will also compare attentional biases across conditions using a between-subjects ANOVA to examine the effect of presentation format (Separate, Simultaneous, Unisensory). 

Finally, we will examine the difference in performance from the final block of training to the generalization test across presentation format conditions using a mixed model ANOVA.
table.inference_criteria: We will use the standard p < .05 criteria for determining if the ANOVA, t-tests, and the post hoc tests suggest that the results are significantly different from those expected if the null hypothesis were correct. The post-hoc Bonferroni test adjusts for multiple comparisons.
table.data_exclusion_criteria: Participants will be excluded from these analyses if they have accuracy less than 85% on attention checks. Attention checks with occur in both auditory and visual modalities for multisensory conditions and only in the trained modality for unisensory conditions. Those in multisensory conditions will be required to have >= 85% accuracy on both auditory and visual attention check trials. Outliers will be included in analyses.
table.missing_data_handling: Analyses will be conducted on all available data and ignore missing data.
table.exploratory_analyses:
We plan to examine the proportion of participants across presentation type conditions who report using different modalities to make categorization decisions based on their overt responses (using Fisher’s exact tests) and how these responses align with participants’ responses to audiovisual-incongruent stimuli with the prediction that if they report attending to a specific modality, their responses to incongruent stimuli should align most with that modality. 

We also plan to compare performance in the auditory and visual Unisensory conditions.

table.title: How Presentation Shapes Multisensory Category Learning
table.research_questions:
1. If the results of our previous study replicate and presentation format does not impact multisensory category learning, there will be no differences in training accuracy when auditory and visual category information is presented simultaneously or separately. 

2. If the results of our previous study replicate and presentation format affects multisensory category generalization, generalization test accuracy will be higher overall when information was presented simultaneously during training compared to separately.  

3. If the results of our previous study replicate and different presentation formats encourage different kinds of attention to stimulus information, there will be a significant interaction between training presentation (simultaneous, separate) and generalization test trial type (audiovisual, auditory-only, visual-only). When information was presented simultaneously during training, participants will perform better in the test when auditory information is present (audiovisual, auditory-only) than when only visual information is present. In contrast, when information was presented separately during training, participants will not perform differently across test trial types. 

4. If the results of our previous study replicate and different presentation formats encourage different kinds of attention to stimulus information, participants trained with information presented simultaneously during training will have responses to incongruent audiovisual stimuli that are more aligned with the auditory stimulus category than the visual stimulus category, while those trained with information presented separately will have responses to incongruent audiovisual stimuli aligned with neither auditory nor visual. We hypothesize that in this higher-powered sample, this difference will be significant indicating an attentional bias in the simultaneous training condition. 

Critically, this new experiment will enable testing different competing hypotheses about the source of this attentional bias: 

A. If multisensory presentation of the information drives the attentional bias, then simultaneous presentation will produce a stronger auditory bias than separate presentation, regardless of whether information was presented at relatively short or long stimulus durations. 

B. If attentional demand due to relatively short stimulus presentation times drives the attentional bias in the simultaneous training condition, then short total stimulus duration (1000 ms) will produce stronger auditory bias than long duration (2000 ms), regardless of whether information was presented simultaneously or separately during training.

C. If multisensory presentation and attentional demand due to relatively short stimulus presentations both impact attentional biases, we may expect:
C1. Significant independent effects of presentation type during training (simultaneous, separate) and presentation duration (short, long). 
C2. Significant interaction between these factors. While there are many possible patterns of interactions, we pose that a likely pattern we would find is that any type of training that presents information separately across modalities will not result in an attention bias (regardless of short or long stimulus presentation) but that training that presents information simultaneously will result in a stronger attention bias when information is presented for a relatively short duration compared to a long duration. 

D. If neither presentation type nor stimulus duration impact attentional biases, we expect to see no differences in accuracy across test trial types and responses that are not aligned with either the auditory or visual modality for incongruent stimuli, with no differences across conditions.
table.study_type: Experiment - A researcher randomly assigns treatments to study subjects, this includes field or lab experiments. This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials.
table.blinding: For studies that involve human subjects, they will not know the treatment group to which they have been assigned. Personnel who interact directly with the study subjects (either human or non-human subjects) will not be aware of the assigned treatments. (Commonly known as “double blind”)
table.study_design_overview: Mixed design varying presentation timing (simultaneous vs. separate, between-subjects) and total duration of stimulus presentation (short vs, long, between-subjects). In training, training block (1-8, within-subjects). In test, stimulus type (auditory, visual, audiovisual, within-subjects) + incongruent audiovisual. We will counterbalance the order of presentation of modalities for separate trials (auditory-visual or visual-auditory), assignment of category to response key mapping (category A = 1 and B = 2 or category A = 2 and B = 1), whether audiovisual test stimuli are presented separately or simultaneously, and the duration (short/long) of the test stimuli.
table.randomization: Participants will be randomly assigned to one of four conditions that vary in presentation timing (Simultaneous, Separate) and total stimulus duration (1000 ms [short], 2000 ms [long]) using a randomization node in Gorilla Experiment Builder (Anwyl-Irvine et al., 2020). Within each participant, trial order in both training and test will be randomized using rowwise randomization in the spreadsheet in Gorilla's Task Builder.
table.existing_data: Registration prior to creation of data
table.data_collection_procedures: Participants will be undergraduate students from the University of New Hampshire, between the ages of 18 to 65, who will participate for partial course credit using the SONA Psychology Subject Pool. Participants will be required to self-report normal or corrected-to-normal hearing and vision.
table.sample_size_rationale: The target number of participants was determined via a series of power analyses using WebPower (Zhang & Yuan, 2018) based on the results of an initial Experiment 1 (which was not pre-registered). We wanted to be sure we can detect the size of effect in the analysis of attention bias across conditions from the audiovisual-incongruent stimuli (d = 0.35) that was not statistically significant in Experiment 1. To detect an effect size of d = 0.35 for an independent samples t-test, with an alpha of .05 and power of 80%, 65 participants would be needed in each condition (Separate and Simultaneous). Next, we wanted to be sure we can detect the most complex interaction in our planned analyses of presentation timing (2, between-subjects), total duration (2, between-subjects), and stimulus type (3, within-subjects). Using the sample size determined from the first power analysis (and rounding to have equal numbers in the groups), with 33 participants per individual condition with alpha of .05, power of 80%, the smallest possible observable interaction effect size we would be able to observe is relatively small (f = 0.16). Therefore, we are confident that this sample size would be able to detect possible a three-way interaction and so we plan to recruit 33 participants per condition for a total of 132 participants.

Mean accuracy and reaction time across each block of 25 trials will be calculated for training. 

Mean accuracy and reaction times for each trial type (auditory only, visual only, audiovisual) will be calculated for the generalization test. We will collapse all trials of these stimulus types (regardless of presentation type or duration) in the main analyses. 

Mean proportion of responses aligned with auditory modality category identity will be calculated for audiovisual incongruent stimuli in the generalization test.
table.statistical_tests:
Training phase. Mixed-model ANOVAs will be conducted to examine the effects of presentation timing (Separate vs. Simultaneous; between-subjects), total duration of stimulus presentation (1000 ms [short] vs. 2000 ms [long]; between-subjects), and block (1-8; within-subjects) on accuracy. Any significant main effects or interactions from the ANOVAs will be explored further with Bonferroni-corrected post-hoc tests.

Test phase. We will examine generalization accuracy using a mixed-model ANOVA with effects of presentation timing (Separate vs. Simultaneous; between-subjects), total duration of stimulus presentation (1000 ms [short] vs. 2000 ms [long]; between-subjects), and trial type (auditory-only, visual-only, audiovisual-congruent; within-subjects). If there are any significant interactions or a main effect of trial type, we will focus our interpretations on comparisons of single modality (auditory-only, visual-only) vs. audiovisual (as evidence of potential multisensory categorization benefits) and auditory-only vs. visual-only (as evidence of attentional bias). 

We will compute the second measure of attentional bias from audiovisual-incongruent trials by using the proportion of responses aligned with the auditory modality minus the proportion of responses aligned with the visual modality. Attentional bias will be assessed within each group separately using one-sample t-tests against chance level (0.50). We will also compare attentional biases across groups using a 2x2 between-subjects ANOVA to examine the effects of presentation timing (Separate vs. Simultaneous) and total duration stimulus presentation (1000 ms [short] vs. 2000 ms [long]).
table.inference_criteria: We will use the standard p < .05 criteria for determining if the ANOVA, t-tests, and the post hoc tests suggest that the results are significantly different from those expected if the null hypothesis were correct. The post-hoc Bonferroni test adjusts for multiple comparisons.
table.data_exclusion_criteria:
We will include attention checks in both auditory and visual modalities where participants will need to rapidly (<2 seconds) press the spacebar when hearing a brief pure tone or seeing a "Press the spacebar" prompt on the screen. We will only include participants who perform above 85% on these attention checks in both modalities.  

Outliers will be included in the analyses.
table.missing_data_handling: If a participant does not complete all category learning and generalization test trials, they will not be included in the analyses.
table.exploratory_analyses: We will analyze whether there were differences based on the counterbalancing of trial types in the test by varying the presentation type (simultaneous, separate) of audiovisual trials (both congruent or incongruent) or the total presentation duration (short/long) of auditory-only, visual-only, or audiovisual trials (both congruent or incongruent). We counterbalanced these variables to ensure that no specific conditions were favored by having test trials that matched the presentation type experienced during training. We have a weak hypothesis that participants may perform better when the stimulus types match what they experienced during training, but will analyze this as an exploratory analysis due to the small number of trials of each type and the likely lack of power to see many-factor interactions beyond those targeted in our main theoretically-driven analyses. We will also examine answers to the post-test questionnaire and how they may relate to the modality bias or learning outcomes as exploratory analyses.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 60 columns across 8 data files.
#### Issues Identified
3 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(File = c("exp1.csv", "exp2.csv", "exp3.csv"), Column = c("response", "response", "response"), Issues = c("#️⃣ Numeric as text — Column is 100% numeric but 1 value cannot be parsed: \"space\"", "#️⃣ Numeric as text — Column is 100% numeric but 1 value cannot be parsed: \"space\"", "#️⃣ Numeric as text — Column is 100% numeric but 1 value cannot be parsed: \"space\"" )), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 20, FALSE) ```
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 8 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

reproducibility_check.summary_text:
-  We assessed AND ran 1 R code file for reproducibility (each in an isolated Docker container).
-  1 of 1 script ran without error when executed.
-  4 installable dependencies detected.
- 1521 statistics stored from the extracted output; 99 of 149 reported tests matched (66.4%).

ethics_statements: All procedures were approved by the IRB at anonymized for review.
This research received approval from the Institutional Review Board at (anonymized for review).
live_data_statements: Experiment 1 Method Participants Participants were 54 undergraduate students from anonymized for review ages 18-22 (16 Men, 38 Women) who participated for partial course credit.

Participants were randomly assigned to one of two conditions that varied in how multisensory category information was presented during training (Simultaneous [10 Men, 17 Women], Separate [6 Men, 21 Women]).
All participants completed an identical generalization test after training.
Participants completed the study in person using the Gorilla Experiment Builder (Anwyl-Irvine et al., 2020).
After stimulus presentation, participants were prompted to respond which category the audiovisual stimuli belonged to by pressing the 1 or 2 keys on the keyboard.
Participants had an unlimited amount of time to respond.
Finally, we added attention checks throughout training to ensure that participants were attending to both modalities throughout the task.
Participants were 132 undergraduate students from anonymized for review ages 18-26 ( 20Men, 112 Women) who completed the study in person for partial course credit.

Participants were randomly assigned to one of four conditions varying in presentation format (Simultaneous, Separate) and total stimulus duration (Short [1 sec], Long [2 sec]): Simultaneous-Long (N = 34; 7 Men, 27 Women), Simultaneous-Short (N = 31; 5 Men, 26 Women), Separate-Long (N = 33; 5 Men, 28 Women), Separate-Short (N = 34; 3 Men, 31 Women).

The test procedure was similar to Experiment 1 except that participants completed more trials overall (auditory-only: N = 32, visual-only; N = 32, audiovisual congruent: N = 32, audiovisual incongruent: N = 32), only near transfer stimuli were used, and presentation and duration were counterbalanced across trials.

At the end of the experiment, as exploratory measures, participants were asked how they used modality information to make decisions during learning and whether they thought the modalities were related to each other (see Supplemental Materials).
Participants were 180 adults recruited online from Prolific ages 18-64 (95 Men, 85 Women) who completed the study online for a small payment ($10).
Participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions varying in presentation format (Simultaneous, Separate, Unisensory).
All participants completed the same test procedure as Experiment 2 with auditory-only, visual-only, audiovisualseparate, and audiovisual-simultaneous trial types.
Participants completed the same exploratory questionnaire measures as Experiment 2 (see Supplementary Materials).

When participants were trained on the visual modality, responses were aligned more with the visual than auditory modality (M = 0.28, t(36) = -8.02, p < .0001, d = -1.32) which was significantly different from all other conditions (ps < .0001).

When participants were trained on the auditory modality (M = 0.67, t(31) = 5.65, p < .0001, d = 1.00) or both modalities Separately (M = 0.62, t(55) = 4.16, p = .00011, d = 0.56) or Simultaneously (M = 0.70, t(54) = 6.79, p < .0001, d = 0.92), responses were aligned more with the auditory than visual modality and this did not differ across conditions (ps > .34).
Consent to participate: All participants gave informed consent prior to participation.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 1 R code file.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 1 script: 1 ran without error, 0 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

info.title: MULTISENSORY CATEGORY LEARNING Costs and Benefits of Multisensory Category Learning

author.affiliation:
Department of Psychology
								University of New Hampshire

Department of Psychology
								University of New Hampshire

text.text: Our conceptual understanding of the world is based on information from multiple senses, yet most studies of how we learn novel categories focus on a single modality.

It is imperative to study multisensory learning not only to capture processes involved in naturalistic learning, but also because multisensory contexts may impact how learners attend to and learn from information in different modalities.
In the current study, we examined how novel category learning is impacted when information is presented in multiple modalities, with two main results.
First, simultaneously presenting auditory and visual information led to better generalization to novel category items compared to presenting identical information separately within the same trial.
Second, multisensory learning could be considered to be better than, worse than, or comparable to unisensory learning, depending on the metric of learning considered.

Together, these findings suggest that the way multisensory information is encountered during training directly impacts learning and that presenting information together results in more flexible representations than presenting it separately.
More broadly, these results demonstrate the necessity of investigating multisensory learning to reveal how attention and learning function in more naturalistic learning contexts.

Category learning is a core cognitive process by which individuals learn to organize stimuli into meaningful groups, allowing for generalization from known categories to novel instances (Ashby & Maddox, 2011; Minda et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Category learning is a core cognitive process by which individuals learn to organize stimuli into meaningful groups, allowing for generalization from known categories to novel instances <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Ashby & Maddox, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Minda et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: When we learn to categorize information in our environment, we usually do not rely on just one sensory modality.
Our knowledge about cats, for example, involves visual appearance, auditory vocalizations, as well as tactile and olfactory experiences.

People rely on redundant (e.g., auditory and visual information cuing a /b/ phoneme) and complementary multisensory cues (e.g., visual appearance of a cat and "meow" sound) to learn across the lifespan (Newell et al., 2023; Shams & Seitz, 2008).
text.formatted: People rely on redundant (e.g., auditory and visual information cuing a /b/ phoneme) and complementary multisensory cues (e.g., visual appearance of a cat and "meow" sound) to learn across the lifespan <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Newell et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Shams & Seitz, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Despite the importance of multisensory information in everyday categorization, relatively little is known about how people learn multisensory categories as most studies of category learning have focused on learning from a single sense, typically vision (Minda et al., 2024; Richler & Palmeri, 2014).
text.formatted: Despite the importance of multisensory information in everyday categorization, relatively little is known about how people learn multisensory categories as most studies of category learning have focused on learning from a single sense, typically vision <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Minda et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Richler & Palmeri, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Beyond relevance to real-world behavior, understanding multisensory learning is also critical because there are reasons to expect that presenting information in multiple modalities may facilitate learning (Mathias & von Kriegstein, 2023; Murray & Shams, 2023).
text.formatted: Beyond relevance to real-world behavior, understanding multisensory learning is also critical because there are reasons to expect that presenting information in multiple modalities may facilitate learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Mathias & von Kriegstein, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Murray & Shams, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Research in recognition memory demonstrates that merely presenting a congruent, redundant sound alongside an image (e.g., cat + "meow") facilitates later recognition of that image (Soto-Faraco & Spence, 2025).
text.formatted: Research in recognition memory demonstrates that merely presenting a congruent, redundant sound alongside an image (e.g., cat + "meow") facilitates later recognition of that image <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Soto-Faraco & Spence, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Even pairing arbitrary shapes with redundant sounds can enhance memory for those shapes (Brunel et al., 2013; Lauzon et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Even pairing arbitrary shapes with redundant sounds can enhance memory for those shapes <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Brunel et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Lauzon et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Similar benefits for multisensory learning have recently been demonstrated in category learning.

For example, incidental learning of visual categories (e.g., cartoon frogs) is enhanced when a category-specific auditory cue (e.g., unique 'croak' sound) is presented during training (Broadbent et al., 2020; Broadbent et al., 2019).
text.formatted: For example, incidental learning of visual categories (e.g., cartoon frogs) is enhanced when a category-specific auditory cue (e.g., unique 'croak' sound) is presented during training <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Broadbent et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Broadbent et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, learning of novel auditory speech categories (e.g., Mandarin tones) is enhanced when a category-specific visual cue (e.g., line or hand gesture matching the pitch direction) is presented during training (Zhen et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Similarly, learning of novel auditory speech categories (e.g., Mandarin tones) is enhanced when a category-specific visual cue (e.g., line or hand gesture matching the pitch direction) is presented during training <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Zhen et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Multisensory training improves generalization to novel unisensory category exemplars (Broadbent et al., 2020), suggesting that this benefit is not simply due to the specific information encountered during learning.
text.formatted: Multisensory training improves generalization to novel unisensory category exemplars <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Broadbent et al., 2020)</ref>, suggesting that this benefit is not simply due to the specific information encountered during learning.

text.text: However, not all studies demonstrate a benefit for multisensory over unisensory category learning (O'Dowd et al., 2025), suggesting the need to understand what underlies multisensory benefits in learning.
text.formatted: However, not all studies demonstrate a benefit for multisensory over unisensory category learning <ref type="bibr">(O'Dowd et al., 2025)</ref>, suggesting the need to understand what underlies multisensory benefits in learning.

text.text: One possible explanation for why multisensory training improves learning when it does is that multisensory information enhances perceptual processing by boosting low-level multisensory integration mechanisms that bind cues together into an integrated percept during learning (Murray & Shams, 2023; Stein & Stanford, 2008).
text.formatted: One possible explanation for why multisensory training improves learning when it does is that multisensory information enhances perceptual processing by boosting low-level multisensory integration mechanisms that bind cues together into an integrated percept during learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Murray & Shams, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Stein & Stanford, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: However, an alternative explanation is that improved performance is not specific to multisensory processing but instead stems from presenting more variable information during encoding (Broadbent et al., 2020; Hendriks et al., 2023).
text.formatted: However, an alternative explanation is that improved performance is not specific to multisensory processing but instead stems from presenting more variable information during encoding <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Broadbent et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Hendriks et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: That is, when people have access to more variable information during learning, regardless of whether information comes from one or multiple modalities, learning is enhanced (Broadbent et al., 2020; Hendriks et al., 2023).
text.formatted: That is, when people have access to more variable information during learning, regardless of whether information comes from one or multiple modalities, learning is enhanced <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Broadbent et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Hendriks et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: In prior work, information presented in the second modality is often completely task irrelevant.
As a result, it remains unclear how people process and learn from information in different modalities when the target of learning itself is multisensory.

This is a particularly relevant problem for categorization where information from multiple modalities can be used to determine the category identity -like hearing the song and seeing appearance of a bird to tell its species or combining visual and tactile information to determine an object's identity.

In the current study, we address two research questions to understand (1) how multisensory learning is impacted by the way information is presented across modalities and (2) how multisensory learning differs from unisensory learning.

To address the first question, across three experiments, we compare learning of multisensory (audiovisual) categories when learners encounter identical information simultaneously or separately across modalities within a trial.

When encountering information simultaneously, learners must process and encode information across modalities at the same time, which also enables multisensory integration due to the temporal coherence of the signals (Stein & Stanford, 2008).
text.formatted: When encountering information simultaneously, learners must process and encode information across modalities at the same time, which also enables multisensory integration due to the temporal coherence of the signals <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Stein & Stanford, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: When encountering information separately, learners process and encode information in a unisensory context and then can combine information across modalities to make a categorization decision.

Critically, in both cases, the categories themselves are multisensory, and learners encounter identical multisensory regularities within and across trials, only differing in how that information is delivered.
We test three competing hypotheses about how simultaneous and separate presentation may impact learning.

First, if multisensory learning benefits are driven by multisensory integration supporting enhanced perceptual processing, then learning should be enhanced when auditory and visual information is presented simultaneously compared to separately.

This result would not be consistent with an encoding variability account (i.e., Hendriks et al., 2023) because the variability in stimulus information is the same, it only differs in how it is presented.
text.formatted: This result would not be consistent with an encoding variability account (i.e., <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Hendriks et al., 2023)</ref> because the variability in stimulus information is the same, it only differs in how it is presented.

text.text: Second, rather than making processing more efficient, presenting multiple pieces of information simultaneously may impair attention, specifically impacting learners' ability to find and use relevant information to make decisions compared to presenting the same information separately when both modalities are given dedicated processing time.
As a result, simultaneous presentation may impair learning over separate.

Finally, because the amount of information is the same in these two contexts, aligning with the encoding variability account, there may be no differences between simultaneous and separate presentation.
To address the second question, in Experiment 3, we directly compare learning in multisensory and completely unisensory contexts to test four alternative hypotheses.
First, multisensory information may facilitate learning over unisensory regardless of how that information is presented.

This would be consistent with an encoding variability perspective as there is more information in both multisensory learning contexts to support performance compared to unisensory (Hendriks et al., 2023; Broadbent et al., 2020).
text.formatted: This would be consistent with an encoding variability perspective as there is more information in both multisensory learning contexts to support performance compared to unisensory <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Hendriks et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Broadbent et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Second, multisensory information may facilitate learning over unisensory only when information is presented simultaneously.
This would be consistent with a multisensory integration perspective as efficient integration only occurs when information is temporally aligned (Meredith et al., 1987; Stein & Stanford, 2008).
text.formatted: This would be consistent with a multisensory integration perspective as efficient integration only occurs when information is temporally aligned <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Meredith et al., 1987;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Stein & Stanford, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Third, if multisensory information in either format poses attentional costs compared to unisensory information (Li & Deng, 2024; Rau et al., 2020; Sandhu & Dyson, 2016), multisensory information may impair learning over unisensory.
text.formatted: Third, if multisensory information in either format poses attentional costs compared to unisensory information <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Li & Deng, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Rau et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Sandhu & Dyson, 2016)</ref>, multisensory information may impair learning over unisensory.

text.text: Finally, it is also possible that multisensory learning may not differ from unisensory, with learners able to extract categoryrelevant information regardless of the context in which it is presented (O'Dowd et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Finally, it is also possible that multisensory learning may not differ from unisensory, with learners able to extract categoryrelevant information regardless of the context in which it is presented <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(O'Dowd et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: To anticipate, across three experiments, we find that simultaneous presentation consistently facilitates generalization to novel category exemplars relative to separate presentation of the same information, supporting a multisensory integration account of learning benefits.
Further, we find that multisensory training can lead to better, worse, or comparable outcomes as unisensory training depending on what aspect of learning is considered.
Together, these results suggest that multisensory training impacts how learners attend to and learn from category information.
Experiment 1 Method Participants Participants were 54 undergraduate students from anonymized for review ages 18-22 (16 Men, 38 Women) who participated for partial course credit.
All participants reported normal or corrected-to-normal vision and hearing.

Participants were randomly assigned to one of two conditions that varied in how multisensory category information was presented during training (Simultaneous [10 Men, 17 Women], Separate [6 Men, 21 Women]).
All participants completed an identical generalization test after training.
Participants completed the study in person using the Gorilla Experiment Builder (Anwyl-Irvine et al., 2020).
All procedures were approved by the IRB at anonymized for review.
All participants learned two multisensory categories comprised of redundant visual and auditory stimuli.
The categories and stimuli for training were identical to a previous study comparing auditory and visual unisensory learning (Roark et al., 2021).
text.formatted: The categories and stimuli for training were identical to a previous study comparing auditory and visual unisensory learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Roark et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Auditory stimuli were 1 sec complex nonspeech ripple sounds varying in temporal (Hz) and spectral modulation (cycles/octave).
Visual stimuli were circular Gabor patches presented on a grey background and varying in spatial frequency (cycles/pixel) and orientation (degrees).
Category distributions were created sampling from a bivariate Gaussian distribution in normalized space and were then transformed into auditory and visual stimulus spaces (Figure 1A-B).
text.formatted: Category distributions were created sampling from a bivariate Gaussian distribution in normalized space and were then transformed into auditory and visual stimulus spaces (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1A-B</ref>).

text.text: Categories were redundant such that they could be distinguished with a unidimensional rule using information in either modality -spatial frequency dimension of the Gabor patches (rule boundary at 0.05 cycles/pixel) or the temporal modulation rate of the ripple sounds (rule boundary at 7.5 Hz).
Stimuli and Task Procedures Note.
A. Colored points represent the training stimuli for the two categories and Xs represent stimuli in the generalization test.
B. Example visual stimulus (top) and spectrogram of auditory stimulus (bottom).
C. Note that order of presentation of modalities in Separate condition was counterbalanced across trials.
There were 100 visual and 100 auditory stimuli (50 per category) presented in the training phase.

A separate set of auditory and visual stimuli were created for the generalization test including both near transfer stimuli sampled in an 8x8 grid in the same space as training stimuli (Xs in Figure 1A; 64 auditory, 64 visual) and far transfer stimuli that were shifted along the category-irrelevant dimensions to test the ability to generalize to dissimilar stimuli from training (spectral modulation: near M = 0.86 cycles per octave, far M = -2.94 cycles per octave; orientation: near M = 54.0 degrees, far M = 109.2 degrees; 64 auditory, 64 visual).
text.formatted: A separate set of auditory and visual stimuli were created for the generalization test including both near transfer stimuli sampled in an 8x8 grid in the same space as training stimuli (Xs in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1A</ref>; 64 auditory, 64 visual) and far transfer stimuli that were shifted along the category-irrelevant dimensions to test the ability to generalize to dissimilar stimuli from training (spectral modulation: near M = 0.86 cycles per octave, far M = -2.94 cycles per octave; orientation: near M = 54.0 degrees, far M = 109.2 degrees; 64 auditory, 64 visual).

text.text: The procedure included both training (200 trials across 8 blocks of 25 trials) and test phases (112 trials across 4 blocks of 28 trials).
Auditory stimuli were presented through Sennheiser over-ear headphones.

Auditory and visual stimuli were presented at the same time in the Simultaneous condition and separately within the same trial in the Separate condition (with modality order counterbalanced across trials; Figure 1C).
text.formatted: Auditory and visual stimuli were presented at the same time in the Simultaneous condition and separately within the same trial in the Separate condition (with modality order counterbalanced across trials; Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1C</ref>).

text.text: Stimuli in both conditions were presented for 1 sec.

To avoid the possible perception of the separately presented auditory and visual stimuli as overlapping due to persistence of stimulus information during the presentation of the second stimulus, Separate trials included a 150 ms interstimulus interval (Bowling & Lovegrove, 1980; Efron, 1970a Efron, , 1970b)).
text.formatted: To avoid the possible perception of the separately presented auditory and visual stimuli as overlapping due to persistence of stimulus information during the presentation of the second stimulus, Separate trials included a 150 ms interstimulus interval <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bowling & Lovegrove, 1980;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Efron, 1970a</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Efron, , 1970b))</ref>.

text.text: After stimulus presentation, participants were prompted to respond which category the audiovisual stimuli belonged to by pressing the 1 or 2 keys on the keyboard.
The assignment of keys to different categories was counterbalanced across participants.
Participants had an unlimited amount of time to respond.
Immediately after their response, participants received feedback (Correct or Incorrect) for 1 sec, followed by a 1 sec inter-trial interval.
In the test phase, participants categorized auditory-only ( 16 trials
text.formatted: In the test phase, participants categorized auditory-only ( <ref type="formula">16 trials</ref>

text.text: Accuracy improved across training (block 1: M = 65%, block 8: M = 81%; p < .0001), indicating successful learning (Figure 2A; F(7, 364) = 16.8, p < .0001, ηG² = 0.11).
text.formatted: Accuracy improved across training (block 1: M = 65%, block 8: M = 81%; p < .0001), indicating successful learning (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2A</ref>; F(7, 364) = 16.8, p < .0001, ηG² = 0.11).

text.text: Training accuracy did not differ across Simultaneous (M = 74%) and Separate conditions (M = 79%; F(1, 52) = 2.77, p = .10, ηG² = 0.032) and condition did not interact with block (F(7, 364) = 1.93, p = .064, ηG² = 0.014).
Note.
Error bars represent SEM.
Horizontal line at 50% represents chance-level performance in left and center panels.
Horizontal line at 0.50 represents responses aligning with neither modality in right panels.
In contrast to training, generalization test accuracy was significantly higher in the Simultaneous (M = 71%) than Separate condition (M = 62%; F(1, 52) = 7.065, p = .010, ηG² = 0.075).

Accuracy also differed across trial types (F(2, 104) = 9.21, p = .00021, ηG² = 0.037), with a significant interaction between condition and trial type (Figure 2B; F(2, 104) = 4.55, p = .013, ηG² = 0.019) which we investigate further with Bonferroni-corrected comparisons.
text.formatted: Accuracy also differed across trial types (F(2, 104) = 9.21, p = .00021, ηG² = 0.037), with a significant interaction between condition and trial type (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2B</ref>; F(2, 104) = 4.55, p = .013, ηG² = 0.019) which we investigate further with Bonferroni-corrected comparisons.

text.text: Performance in the Simultaneous condition was significantly better than the Separate condition for auditory-only (Mdifference = 12%, p < .0001) and audiovisual trials (Mdifference = 12%, p < .0001), and conditions did not differ on visual-only trials (Mdifference = 3%, p = .26).
text.formatted: Performance in the Simultaneous condition was significantly better than the Separate condition for auditory-only (Mdifference = 12%, p < .0001) and audiovisual trials (Mdifference = 12%, p < .0001), and conditions did not differ on visual-only trials (Mdifference = 3%, p = .26).

text.text: For the Simultaneous condition, test performance was worse when only visual information was presented (M = 64%) compared to when only auditory (M = 73%; p = .0020) or audiovisual information was presented (M = 76%; p < .0001).
text.formatted: For the Simultaneous condition, test performance was worse when only visual information was presented (M = 64%) compared to when only auditory (M = 73%; p = .0020) or audiovisual information was presented (M = 76%; p < .0001).

text.text: Auditory only and audiovisual trials did not differ (p = .41).
In contrast, for the Separate condition, performance did not differ across trial types (audiovisual: M = 63%, auditory: M = 61%, visual: M = 61%, ps > .51).
text.formatted: In contrast, for the Separate condition, performance did not differ across trial types (audiovisual: M = 63%, auditory: M = 61%, visual: M = 61%, ps > .51).

text.text: Conditions also differed in how they responded to incongruent auditory and visual information.

While responses in the Simultaneous condition were more strongly aligned with the auditory than visual modality (Figure 2C; M = 0.64; t(26) = 3.82, p = .00074, d = 0.74), responses in the Separate condition did not clearly align with either modality (M = 0.57; t(26) = 1.85, p = .075, d = 0.36).
text.formatted: While responses in the Simultaneous condition were more strongly aligned with the auditory than visual modality (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2C</ref>; M = 0.64; t(26) = 3.82, p = .00074, d = 0.74), responses in the Separate condition did not clearly align with either modality (M = 0.57; t(26) = 1.85, p = .075, d = 0.36).

text.text: Though the conditions demonstrated different patterns, the conditions were not significantly different (M = 0.07; t(51.9) = 1.30, p = .20, d = 0.35).
In Experiment 1, we found that the way identical category information was presented impacted how learners attended to and learned multisensory categories.
Specifically, simultaneous presentation resulted in better generalization performance than separate, particularly on audiovisual and auditory-only trials.
These results support a multisensory integration account of learning benefits, but there are some aspects of our design that prevent us from drawing firm conclusions.
We address these aspects in Experiment 2.
To account for possible alternative explanations for the results in Experiment 1, we made several changes to Experiment 2.

First, while stimuli in the two conditions were identical, conditions differed in both how stimuli were presented and the total stimulus duration such that differences could be due to the relatively short time Simultaneous learners had to process the stimuli (1 sec) compared to Separate learners (1 sec + 1 sec = 2 sec).
In Experiment 2, we disentangle these explanations by separately manipulating presentation format and stimulus duration.
Second, all audiovisual test stimuli were presented simultaneously, potentially introducing an unintended familiarity benefit in the Simultaneous condition.
In Experiment 2, we counterbalance the presentation and duration of test trials to not unfairly advantage any condition.
Third, while the pattern of responses for incongruent stimuli was qualitatively different in the two conditions (d = 0.35), the overall effect was not significant.
Given the observed effect size, we were underpowered to observe a difference (sensitivity analysis indicated that our sample size could detect an effect of d = 0.78 or larger with 80% power).
In Experiment 2, we collect a higher-powered sample given the effect sizes observed in Experiment 1.
Finally, we added attention checks throughout training to ensure that participants were attending to both modalities throughout the task.
Experiment 2 was pre-registered and we report all planned confirmatory analyses (https://osf.io/meuyh/overview?view_only=a029de89132248439c6c35b4968a0bed).

text.text: Participants all reported normal or corrected-to-normal vision and hearing.

Participants were randomly assigned to one of four conditions varying in presentation format (Simultaneous, Separate) and total stimulus duration (Short [1 sec], Long [2 sec]): Simultaneous-Long (N = 34; 7 Men, 27 Women), Simultaneous-Short (N = 31; 5 Men, 26 Women), Separate-Long (N = 33; 5 Men, 28 Women), Separate-Short (N = 34; 3 Men, 31 Women).

According to the power analysis outlined in the preregistration, our final sample had 132 participants after exclusion of 56 participants due to failure of auditory and visual attention checks (< 85% accuracy on both types).

text.text: Experiment 2 included the same training stimuli and the near transfer test stimuli from Experiment 1.
Auditory stimuli durations were 0.5, 1, or 2 sec depending on condition.

The training procedure was similar to Experiment 1 except that conditions also varied in the total stimulus duration -relatively Short (Separate: 0.5 sec + 0.5 sec; Simultaneous: 1 sec) or Long (Separate: 1 sec + 1 sec; Simultaneous: 2 sec).
Simultaneous-Short and Separate-Long conditions are identical to the conditions from Experiment 1.

Additionally, attention check trials occurred five times each in every training block and required pressing the spacebar within 2 sec after hearing a 2 sec 1000 Hz pure tone or seeing a visual cue to press the spacebar.

The test procedure was similar to Experiment 1 except that participants completed more trials overall (auditory-only: N = 32, visual-only; N = 32, audiovisual congruent: N = 32, audiovisual incongruent: N = 32), only near transfer stimuli were used, and presentation and duration were counterbalanced across trials.

At the end of the experiment, as exploratory measures, participants were asked how they used modality information to make decisions during learning and whether they thought the modalities were related to each other (see Supplemental Materials).
Accuracy improved across training, indicating successful learning (Figure 2D; F(7, 896) = 35.3, p < .0001, ηG² = 0.098; block 1: M = 63%; block 8: M = 78%, p < .0001).

text.text: As in Experiment 1, training accuracy did not differ across Simultaneous (M = 74%) and Separate conditions (M = 73%; F(1, 128) = 0.29, p = .59, ηG² = 0.001).
Training accuracy was better when stimuli were presented for relatively long (M = 77%) compared to short durations (M = 71%; F(1, 128) = 6.14, p = .015, ηG² = 0.028).

As in Experiment 1, there was a significant interaction between training condition and test trial type (F(3, 384) = 2.99, p = .031, ηG² = 0.0080).
Performance in the Simultaneous condition was significantly better than the Separate condition across all trial types (ps < .00047).

text.text: Surprisingly, performance was 10% better in the Simultaneous condition (M = 82%) for audiovisual-separate trials that exactly matched the training format for the Separate condition (M = 72%).

To contextualize this surprising finding, we conducted an additional exploratory analysis comparing accuracy in the final training block with the two types of audiovisual test trials in the two conditions.
There was a significant interaction between training condition and trial type (F(2, 256) = 24.7, p < .0001, ηG² = 0.067).

Performance was impaired when only visual information was presented (M = 58%) compared to both audiovisual test trial types (ps < .031) but was only impaired when auditory information was presented (M = 64%) compared to audiovisual-separate trials (p = .00075; auditory-only vs. audiovisual-simultaneous: p = 1.0).

text.text: In contrast to Experiment 1, in this higher-powered study, responses to incongruent audiovisual stimuli significantly differed across conditions (F(1, 128) = 5.78, p = .018, ηG² = 0.043) -responses were more strongly aligned with the auditory modality after Simultaneous (M = 0.66) than Separate training (M = 0.57).
Responses did not differ across training duration (F(1,128) = 1.28, p = .26, ηG² = 0.10) or the interaction between presentation and duration (F(1,128) = 0.18, p = .67, ηG² = 0.001).
Experiment 2 replicated the effects of Experiment 1 while also controlling for potential confounds.
In Experiment 2, simultaneous presentation resulted in better generalization performance than separate for all trial types and encouraged learners to rely more on auditory than visual information.
These results support a multisensory integration account of learning benefits as learning was enhanced when identical information was presented simultaneously.
Critically, it remains unclear how these multisensory conditions compare to unisensory learning.
We address this directly in Experiment 3.
In Experiment 3, we replicate comparisons of Separate and Simultaneous training in a broader participant sample collected online and directly compare multisensory to unisensory training.
To simplify comparisons and because duration did not impact test performance, total stimulus duration was held constant across conditions (2 sec).
Experiment 3 was pre-registered and we report all planned confirmatory analyses (https://osf.io/ugp34/overview?view_only=4d1dc6d0812d40398617d3027ce21725).
