text.text: Participants were 180 adults recruited online from Prolific ages 18-64 (95 Men, 85 Women) who completed the study online for a small payment ($10).
Participants all reported normal or corrected-to-normal vision and hearing.
Participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions varying in presentation format (Simultaneous, Separate, Unisensory).

There were 55 participants in the Simultaneous condition (18-53 years, 30 Men, 25 Women), 56 participants in the Separate condition (18-64 years, 29 Men, 27 Women), and 69 participants in the Unisensory condition (18-62 years, 36 Men, 33 Women).
Per the power analysis outlined in the pre-registration, our final sample had 180 participants after exclusion of 37 participants due to failure of auditory and/or visual attention checks.
Stimuli were identical to Experiment 2.
Stimuli were presented for relatively long durations with a total stimulus duration of 2 sec.
The training procedures for the Simultaneous and Separate conditions were identical to the long duration conditions from Experiment 2.
In the Unisensory condition, participants only encountered information in one modality, with the trained modality (auditory, visual) counterbalanced across participants.
The same attention checks were used as Experiment 2.
Unisensory condition attention checks were only given in the trained modality.
All participants completed the same test procedure as Experiment 2 with auditory-only, visual-only, audiovisualseparate, and audiovisual-simultaneous trial types.

In the Unisensory conditions, test performance in the untrained modality was significantly but weakly better than chance (M = 56%, t(68) = 3.90, p < .0001, d = 0.47), but training performance did not significantly differ across auditory and visual modalities (t(61.9) = 1.26, p = .21, d = 0.30).

text.text: Condition did not interact with block (F(14, 1239) = 0.54, p = .91, ηG² = 0.003).
Overall test performance differed across conditions (F(2, 177) = 4.34, p = .014, ηG² = 0.47).
As in prior experiments, generalization test accuracy was significantly higher in the Simultaneous (M = 75%) than Separate condition (M = 69%, p = .030).
Simultaneous multisensory learning resulted in better test performance than Unisensory learning (M = 69%, p = .036), while Separate multisensory learning was comparable to Unisensory (p = 1.0).
However, these results were driven by differences in the untrained modality.

When removing untrained modality trials, conditions still differed (F(2, 177) = 4.30, p = .015, ηG² = 0.046), but test performance was comparable in Simultaneous (M = 75%) and Unisensory conditions (M = 76%, p = 1.0) and worse in Separate (M = 69%) than the Unisensory condition (p = .021).

To investigate the impact of test trial type and the interaction with condition, we slightly deviated from our planned analysis to enable treating test trial type as a fully within-subjects variable -instead of collapsing across Unisensory conditions, we examined auditory and visual Unisensory conditions separately.

As in previous experiments, accuracy differed across trial types (Figure 2H; F(3, 528) = 34.0, p < .0001, ηG² = 0.066) and this effect significantly interacted with condition (F(9, 528) = 16.9, p < .0001, ηG² = 0.095).

text.text: In examining how presentation format impacts multisensory learning, we found that performance was significantly better in the Simultaneous than Separate conditions, but this pattern was only significant for visual-only trials (Mdifference = 8%, p = .040), with no differences in other trial types after correcting for multiple comparisons (auditory-only: Mdifference = 5%, p = .38; audiovisual-simultaneous: Mdifference = 8%, p = .12; audiovisual-separate: Mdifference = 5%, p = .96).
In comparing unisensory and multisensory learning, we found that effects depended on trial type.

When training was unisensory or multisensory, performance did not differ across auditory-only (Unisensory-auditory: M =74%; Separate: 73%, p = 1.0; Simultaneous: M = 78%; p = .96) or audiovisual trials (ps > .14) but performance was much better in visual-only trials when training was unisensory (Unisensory-visual: M = 79%; Separate: M = 59%, p < .0001; Simultaneous: M = 67%, p = .0044).
text.formatted: When training was unisensory or multisensory, performance did not differ across auditory-only (Unisensory-auditory: M =74%; Separate: 73%, p = 1.0; Simultaneous: M = 78%; p = .96) or audiovisual trials (ps > .14) but performance was much better in visual-only trials when training was unisensory (Unisensory-visual: M = 79%; Separate: M = 59%, p < .0001; Simultaneous: M = 67%, p = .0044).

text.text: When participants learned Unisensory categories, they successfully generalized to both unisensory and multisensory stimuli.

Performance on trained-modality trials (auditory: M = 74%; visual = M = 79%) was not different from audiovisual trials (auditory: separate: M = 73% vs. simultaneous: M = 76%; visual: separate: M = 76% vs. simultaneous: M = 77%; ps > .99).

text.text: Different from Experiment 2, when participants learned multisensory categories either Separately or Simultaneously, learning similarly generalized to audiovisual trials that matched or were different from the training format for both Simultaneous (separate: 81% vs. simultaneous: 81%, p = 1.0) and Separate conditions (separate M = 76% vs. simultaneous: M = 73%, p = .48).

In both conditions, performance also did not differ across auditory-only and audiovisual trials (Separate: M = 73%, ps > .50; Simultaneous: M = 78%, ps > .70), but performance was significantly worse on visual-only trials than all other trial types (Separate: M = 59%, ps < .0001; Simultaneous: M = 67%, ps < .00058).

As in Experiment 2, there was a significant interaction between condition and trial type (F(4, 354) = 7.68, p < .0001, ηG² = 0.025).

Conditions differed in how they responded to incongruent stimuli (F(3, 176) = 36.5, p < .0001, ηG² = 0.38).

text.text: When participants were trained on the visual modality, responses were aligned more with the visual than auditory modality (M = 0.28, t(36) = -8.02, p < .0001, d = -1.32) which was significantly different from all other conditions (ps < .0001).

text.text: This suggests that multisensory training -Separate or Simultaneous -encourages attention to the auditory over the visual modality, resulting in impaired visual-only test performance.

In Experiment 3, we replicated a core finding from Experiment 2 in a broader sample of participants who completed the tasks online -multisensory learning with simultaneous presentation resulted in better generalization to novel exemplars than separate presentation.
However, rather than an across-the-board benefit, the benefit was restricted to visual-only trials and better preservation of performance from training to test.
Inclusion of unisensory conditions further clarified the locus of these benefits.
Multisensory training did not uniformly enhance learning over unisensory -performance was comparable, better, or worse in unisensory contexts depending on the type of information being categorized.

Across three experiments, we found that simultaneous presentation of redundant auditory and visual category information resulted in better test performance than when the same information was presented separately.
We also found that multisensory learning resulted in comparable, better, or worse outcomes than unisensory learning depending on the information available in the test.
These results suggest that multisensory learning can introduce both costs and benefits as learners prioritize information in one modality over the other.
The benefits are higher and costs lower when multisensory information is presented simultaneously rather than separately.
All experiments demonstrated that Simultaneous presentation led to better test outcomes than Separate, though the nature of the benefits differed somewhat across experiments.

In general, these results support a multisensory integration perspective, such that synchronous multisensory signals are integrated in low-level perceptual processing (Meredith et al., 1987; Stein & Stanford, 2008), so receiving the same information simultaneously is more advantageous than receiving it separately.
text.formatted: In general, these results support a multisensory integration perspective, such that synchronous multisensory signals are integrated in low-level perceptual processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Meredith et al., 1987;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Stein & Stanford, 2008)</ref>, so receiving the same information simultaneously is more advantageous than receiving it separately.

text.text: This result does not support the explanation that learning benefits from higher encoding variability because the information was identical, only varying in how it was presented within a trial.
We next address other potential explanations for the benefits of simultaneous over separate multisensory learning.
Our results also suggest a distinction between learning (i.e., performance in training) and outcomes of learning (i.e., performance in generalization test).
While the conditions did not differ in performance during training, Simultaneous training facilitated generalization performance over Separate.
These different patterns in training and test are due to preservation of performance in the Simultaneous condition and deterioration in the Separate condition.
In the test, participants no longer received feedback and encountered unisensory stimuli and audiovisual stimuli presented differently than what they encountered during training.
One possible explanation for these results is that Separate presentation may have increased the cognitive load of the task.

Because information was presented separately in time, participants may have intentionally held information about the first stimulus in working memory while processing the second stimulus, which could have impaired learning (Miles & Minda, 2011; Zeithamova & Maddox, 2006).
text.formatted: Because information was presented separately in time, participants may have intentionally held information about the first stimulus in working memory while processing the second stimulus, which could have impaired learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Miles & Minda, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Zeithamova & Maddox, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: While this did not disrupt performance during training, by engaging these resources, participants may have become more fatigued, impairing performance on the final task of the experiment (i.e., generalization test).

Further, because we counterbalanced the order of auditory and visual stimuli across trials, participants may have subjectively experienced different trials as switching between different tasks, which may have added additional cognitive load that could have impaired learning (Dubravac et al., 2026; Erickson, 2008; Roark, 2025).
text.formatted: Further, because we counterbalanced the order of auditory and visual stimuli across trials, participants may have subjectively experienced different trials as switching between different tasks, which may have added additional cognitive load that could have impaired learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Dubravac et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Erickson, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Roark, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: To explore this possibility, we compared the time it took participants to complete the tasks with the assumption that taking longer would be associated with additional cognitive demand and fatigue (Chen et al., 2011).
text.formatted: To explore this possibility, we compared the time it took participants to complete the tasks with the assumption that taking longer would be associated with additional cognitive demand and fatigue <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Chen et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: It took participants significantly longer to complete the Separate (M = 23.3 minutes) than Simultaneous condition (M = 20.5 minutes, t(47.1) = 2.92, p = .0053, d = 0.80), but only in Experiment 1.
There were no differences in completion time across conditions in Experiments 2 or 3 (see Supplemental Materials).
This does not eliminate the possibility of differences in cognitive load across conditions, but it does not strongly support it either.

The persistent deterioration in performance from training to test may also suggest that Separate learners are particularly sensitive to changes in how information is presented because of how they expect information to unfold over time.
In the test, when one modality was presented, it may or may not have been followed by a second modality.

Because Separate learners were used to receiving information in one modality and then the other, when information in the relatively weak visual modality was presented, learners may have expected auditory to follow it and when it did not come, they could not retroactively change how they attended to visual information to make an accurate decision.
Thus, this resulted in impaired performance on visual-only trials compared to audiovisual-separate trials.

Similarly, in the test, if both modalities were presented simultaneously, Separate learners unaccustomed to encountering information in this way may have been overwhelmed, unable to extract key information to make an accurate decision.

While Unisensory learners would simply need to ignore additional apparently irrelevant modality information, Separate learners may expect the information to come separately with dedicated processing time and now must process the same information rapidly together.
Thus, audiovisualsimultaneous trials have increased attentional costs compared to audiovisual-separate because the presentation format violated their expectations.

Though this detriment in audiovisualsimultaneous trials for Separate relative to Simultaneous training was statistically significant in Experiments 1 (-12%) and 2 (-17%), the pattern was present (-8%) but did not survive correction for multiple comparisons in Experiment 3.
However, this pattern suggests a potential benefit for Simultaneous learning in that it may result in more flexible attention when learners encounter information in different formats than training.

It is possible that providing information about which modality or modalities will be presented on the upcoming trial or informing learners during learning that they would later encounter information in different formats might enable Separate learners to overcome this impairment if it is due to violations of expectations.
This remains a topic for future work.
We found that multisensory learning was comparable, better, and worse than unisensory learning depending on how learning was defined.
This indicates that understanding the potential costs and benefits to multisensory over unisensory learning requires defining the target of learning.

If the target of learning is performance on both modalities individually and together, simultaneous multisensory learning is best as it enables the highest accuracy across all kinds of stimuli -auditory, visual, and audiovisual.

If the target of learning is performance in one modality, simultaneous multisensory or unisensory learning are preferable to separate multisensory learning as both led to high accuracy on unisensory trials.
However, if the target of learning is performance in one specific modality, then unisensory learning is best.
While auditory learning was similar in unisensory and multisensory contexts, visual learning was impaired in multisensory contexts as learners prioritized information in the auditory modality.
Our results suggest that presenting information in multiple modalities impacts how learners attend to information during learning.
Here, multisensory learning encouraged attention to the auditory modality particularly when information was presented simultaneously.
Recall that optimal performance in this task could be achieved by attending to either or both auditory and visual modalities.
Thus, it is not inherently surprising that learners primarily made decisions based on only one modality.
However, this apparently rational attention strategy came at a cost of impaired visual learning compared to when learning was unisensory.

At first glance, these results seem to conflict with prior work demonstrating that when redundant information across modalities is presented simultaneously, people (especially adults) rely more on the visual modality (Barnhart et al., 2018; Colavita, 1974; Colavita & Weisberg, 1979; Robinson & Sloutsky, 2004).
text.formatted: At first glance, these results seem to conflict with prior work demonstrating that when redundant information across modalities is presented simultaneously, people (especially adults) rely more on the visual modality <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Barnhart et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Colavita, 1974;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Colavita & Weisberg, 1979;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Robinson & Sloutsky, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: One possible explanation for these differences is that we presented stimuli for relatively short durations (0.5-2 sec).

Because auditory information is inherently fleeting, people can successfully process very rapid auditory information (Penney et al., 2000; Shamma, 2001), when information is presented at relatively short durations, auditory learning is often preserved while visual performance is impaired (Emberson et al., 2010) and decisions are less dominated by vision (Ciraolo et al., 2020; Robinson & Sloutsky, 2019).
text.formatted: Because auditory information is inherently fleeting, people can successfully process very rapid auditory information <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Penney et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Shamma, 2001)</ref>, when information is presented at relatively short durations, auditory learning is often preserved while visual performance is impaired <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Emberson et al., 2010)</ref> and decisions are less dominated by vision <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Ciraolo et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Robinson & Sloutsky, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Most studies of visual category learning present the visual stimulus until the participant responds (e.g., Crossley et al., 2025) and when visual information is presented at shorter durations, accuracy tends to be impacted (Roark et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Most studies of visual category learning present the visual stimulus until the participant responds (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Crossley et al., 2025)</ref> and when visual information is presented at shorter durations, accuracy tends to be impacted <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Roark et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Interestingly, varying the duration of stimulus presentation in Experiment 2 did not impact how learners attended to one modality over the other.
Future studies should examine performance at longer durations to understand the driving factors of auditory dominance in category learning.
Together, these results suggest that when considering which format is most beneficial for learning, it is essential to understand the intended learning goal.

While prior studies of multisensory learning often introduce a second modality as a task-irrelevant feature and do not always assess learning in the second modality, this may limit our understanding of the potential costs and benefits to multisensory learning when the target of learning is inherently multisensory.

This is critical as many real-world categories are not simply unisensory categories that may benefit from incidental information in another modality -categories like bird species, rock types, or even speech categories are inherently multisensory.

Our results suggest that presenting multisensory information has broader consequences for learning than have previously been considered, particularly in impacting how people attend to information across modalities.

Our results expand understanding of multisensory learning by demonstrating that depending on the target of learning and the way information is presented across modalities, multisensory learning can benefit, impair, or be comparable to learning from a single modality.
These results also pose significant challenges for current theories of category learning, which do not explicitly account for learning across different sensory modalities.

Most audiovisual trials were congruent (auditory and visual stimuli signal same category identity, N = 32: near transfer: N = 16, far transfer: N = 16) and some were incongruent (auditory and visual stimuli signal different category identities, N = 16, all near transfer).
Audiovisual test stimuli were always presented simultaneously in the test.
The trial procedure was similar to training except that participants did not receive any feedback.

For incongruent audiovisual stimuli, we examined how participants resolved incongruent information by computing the proportion of responses aligned with the category indicated by the auditory stimulus such that values > 0.50 indicate stronger use of auditory information, values < 0.5 indicate stronger use of visual information, and values around 0.50 indicate similar use of both modalities.
